title: PC Randomly Restarts
cardText: Diagnose computers that restart unexpectedly during gaming, normal use, startup or idle periods.
Investigate Windows event logs, overheating, power supply stability, RAM, drivers and storage.
Distinguish Windows crashes from power loss and hardware instability.
text: This guide is for Windows computers that restart unexpectedly without a normal shutdown.
Identify the restart pattern and inspect Windows event logs for useful diagnostic evidence.
Check temperatures, power delivery and memory stability before replacing components.
Investigate drivers, recent changes and storage errors where appropriate.
If the computer displays a blue-screen stop code, record it and use the relevant diagnostics.

checkRestartPattern.title: Identify the restart pattern
body: Establish whether the restarts happen during gaming, rendering, startup, sleep, idle periods or ordinary Windows use.
Note whether the computer immediately loses power, displays a blue screen or performs a normal Windows restart.
Check whether the problem began after a hardware, software or driver change.
A restart under sustained load may suggest thermal or power instability, while a restart accompanied by a stop code provides a different diagnostic path.
Check system temperatures first if failures occur mainly under load; otherwise inspect the Windows event logs.

checkTemperatures.title: Check CPU and GPU temperatures
body: Use the manufacturer's monitoring utility or a reputable hardware monitoring tool to view CPU and GPU temperatures.
Observe temperatures at idle and during normal workloads that previously caused problems.
Compare readings with the processor and graphics card manufacturer's operating limits.
Check for thermal throttling, unusually high sustained temperatures or fans failing to respond to increased load.
Temperature limits vary by CPU and GPU model; do not treat a single generic temperature as a universal failure threshold.
Avoid prolonged stress testing if the computer is already overheating or repeatedly losing power.

link.name: Intel: Processor overheating troubleshooting
link.description: Official guidance for identifying thermal throttling, unexpected shutdowns and cooling faults.

resolveCoolingIssue.title: Resolve cooling or overheating problem
body: Inspect vents, heatsinks and fans for dust buildup or airflow restrictions.
Confirm that the CPU and GPU cooling fans operate correctly.
For desktops, inspect case airflow and the installation of the CPU cooler.
If the cooler has recently been removed or installed, check its mounting pressure and thermal interface according to manufacturer instructions.
For laptops, check that vents are unobstructed and fans are operating normally.
After correcting the cooling problem, monitor temperatures and retest system stability.
If temperatures return to normal but restarts continue, investigate the Windows logs.

link.name: Intel: Troubleshoot processor overheating
link.description: Manufacturer guidance for checking cooling systems and thermal problems.

checkEventViewer.title: Inspect Windows restart events
body: Press Windows + R, enter eventvwr.msc and press Enter.
Open Windows Logs, System.
Check the events immediately before and after the most recent unexpected restart.
Look for Kernel-Power Event ID 41, EventLog Event ID 6008, BugCheck Event ID 1001 and User32 Event ID 1074 where present.
Event ID 41 records that Windows did not shut down cleanly. It does not, by itself, identify a faulty power supply.
Event ID 1001 may contain a stop code from a Windows crash.
Event ID 1074 may identify a planned restart initiated by Windows Update, software or a user.
Record relevant timestamps, error codes and source names rather than assuming every warning is related.

link.name: Microsoft: Troubleshoot Kernel-Power Event ID 41
link.description: Explains what Event ID 41 records and how to interpret its diagnostic information.

link.name: Microsoft: Diagnose unexpected restarts using event logs
link.description: Reference for restart-related Event IDs, including 41, 1001, 1074 and 6008.

checkEventViewer.alt: Windows Event Viewer System log showing restart-related Event IDs including 41, 1074 and 6008
checkEventViewer.caption: Check events around the restart time. Event ID 41 confirms an unexpected shutdown but does not identify its cause.

investigateLoggedIssue.title: Investigate the recorded restart cause
body: Check the source and details of the event recorded around the restart.
If Event ID 1074 identifies an update or application-initiated restart, investigate that process.
If Event ID 1001 reports a bugcheck, record the stop code and investigate the associated driver or system crash.
If WHEA-Logger reports hardware errors, record the event details and check the relevant hardware.
If only Event ID 41 or 6008 appears, continue investigating power, thermal and hardware stability.
Do not replace a power supply based solely on a Kernel-Power 41 event.

link.name: Microsoft: Event ID 41 diagnostic interpretation
link.description: Explains how to distinguish stop errors, sudden power interruptions and incomplete shutdowns.

link.name: Microsoft: Unexpected restart and stop code troubleshooting
link.description: Official guidance for Windows crashes, stop codes and recurring unexpected restarts.

repairLoggedIssue.title: Address the identified error
body: Apply the corrective action supported by the specific error or stop code.
For driver-related crashes, investigate the identified driver before changing unrelated software.
For update-related restarts, check update history and installation status.
For hardware error reports, perform the relevant hardware diagnostics.
Make one change at a time and monitor whether unexpected restarts continue.

checkPowerSupply.title: Check power supply stability
body: Consider whether the restarts occur when CPU or GPU power demand increases.
For desktops, check the PSU's wattage, age, compatibility and power connections.
Check that motherboard and graphics card power connectors are fully seated.
Look for damaged power cables, loose connections or evidence of overheating.
Check for GPU power adapters or extension cables that may be loose or incorrectly installed.
If possible, test the desktop with a known-working compatible power supply.
For laptops, investigate charger wattage, battery condition and charging interruptions where relevant.
Do not assume that sudden restarts or Kernel-Power 41 events prove the PSU is defective.
Never open a power supply casing.

link.name: Microsoft: Event ID 41 and possible power interruptions
link.description: Explains how unexpected power loss can generate Event ID 41 and what additional evidence is needed.

replacePsu.title: Power supply fault confirmed
body: Testing with a known-working compatible power supply has resolved the unexpected restarts, or other reliable diagnostics have identified a PSU fault.
Replace the defective desktop power supply with a suitable unit.
Check its capacity and required motherboard and graphics card connectors.
When replacing a modular PSU, use only cables approved for that specific PSU model.
Do not reuse incompatible modular power supply cables.
Retest the computer under normal workloads after replacement.

checkMemory.title: Test system memory
body: Press Windows + R, enter mdsched.exe and press Enter.
Save open work and select Restart now and check for problems.
Allow Windows Memory Diagnostic to complete its tests.
Review the reported results after Windows starts.
If memory errors are found, investigate the RAM modules, memory slots and configuration.
On desktop systems, testing one RAM module at a time can help isolate the fault.
If XMP or EXPO is enabled, temporarily testing with supported default memory settings may help identify an unstable configuration.
A completed test without errors reduces suspicion of a memory fault but does not rule out intermittent RAM problems.

link.name: Microsoft: Unexpected restart troubleshooting
link.description: Official guidance for investigating Windows crashes and hardware-related instability.

checkMemory.alt: Windows Memory Diagnostic dialog with the Restart now and check for problems option
checkMemory.caption: Run Windows Memory Diagnostic to check for memory errors that may cause crashes and restarts.

investigateMemoryFault.title: Isolate the memory fault
body: Record the memory diagnostic errors.
For desktops, test individual RAM modules in a known-working compatible slot where possible.
Check the motherboard manual for recommended memory slots and supported configurations.
Temporarily disable XMP or EXPO if memory instability may be related to overclocked settings.
If an error follows a particular RAM module, that module may be faulty.
If errors follow a particular slot or occur only with multiple modules, investigate the motherboard or memory configuration.
Do not replace RAM solely because one test failed while an unstable overclock was enabled.

replaceMemory.title: Memory fault identified
body: Testing has isolated a defective RAM module or an unsupported memory configuration.
Replace the faulty module with compatible memory if a physical defect is confirmed.
If the problem is caused by unstable XMP or EXPO settings, use stable supported memory settings instead.
Retest memory and computer stability after making changes.
If the errors persist with known-working RAM, investigate the motherboard and memory controller.

checkDrivers.title: Check drivers and Windows crash history
body: Review Windows Update history and any driver changes made before the restarts began.
Open Device Manager and check for devices reporting driver errors.
Pay particular attention to graphics, chipset, storage and network drivers where the evidence points to them.
Check the computer or component manufacturer's support website for compatible drivers.
If the restarts began immediately after a driver update, consider rolling back that driver.
Do not update every driver indiscriminately when there is no evidence that it is involved.

link.name: Microsoft: Update or roll back drivers
link.description: Official instructions for updating, reinstalling and rolling back Windows device drivers.

link.name: Microsoft: Troubleshoot unexpected Windows restarts
link.description: Guidance for driver-related stop codes and recurring crashes.

repairDriverIssue.title: Repair the affected driver
body: Identify the driver that is linked to the unexpected restarts.
Update, roll back or reinstall that driver using the manufacturer's recommended version.
If the problem began after a graphics driver update, test the previous stable driver where appropriate.
Restart the computer and monitor stability.
If the computer continues restarting, investigate other recent changes.

link.name: Microsoft: Driver rollback and reinstall
link.description: Official Device Manager procedures for repairing problematic drivers.

checkRecentChanges.title: Check recent hardware and software changes
body: Determine whether the restarts began after installing new hardware, software, a Windows update or changing BIOS settings.
Check whether any new RAM, GPU, storage device or USB peripheral was added shortly before the problem started.
Review recently installed applications and system utilities.
If overclocking, undervolting, XMP or EXPO settings were changed, consider temporarily returning to supported default settings.
Change one relevant item at a time to establish whether it affects stability.

undoRecentChange.title: Reverse the suspected change
body: Revert the hardware, software, driver or configuration change most closely associated with the beginning of the problem.
For recently installed hardware, remove or disconnect it safely when practical.
Restore stable default overclocking or memory settings where appropriate.
For recent Windows software changes, consider the relevant supported recovery or rollback option.
Retest normal operation before making additional changes.

link.name: Microsoft: Windows unexpected restart troubleshooting
link.description: Official guidance for resolving crashes associated with newly installed hardware and software.

checkDiskHealth.title: Check SSD or HDD health
body: Inspect Windows System event logs for recurring disk, storage controller or filesystem errors.
Use a suitable manufacturer diagnostic utility to review SSD or HDD health and SMART information.
Look for reported media errors, critical warnings, failing health tests or repeated I/O failures.
Check that drive cables and connectors are secure on desktop systems.
Storage errors may contribute to crashes, but a random restart is not by itself evidence of a failing drive.
Back up important files before performing further tests if storage failure is suspected.

replaceStorage.title: Storage fault identified
body: Storage diagnostics or repeated I/O errors indicate a possible failing SSD or HDD.
Back up important data immediately if it remains accessible.
Confirm the affected drive before replacing hardware.
Replace the failing device with a compatible drive when necessary.
Restore data or reinstall the operating system as appropriate.
Retest system stability after repairing the storage fault.

checkBiosFirmware.title: Check BIOS and firmware stability
body: Check whether the system is running with unstable overclocking, undervolting or memory settings.
Compare the installed BIOS version with the computer or motherboard manufacturer's support information.
Review available BIOS and firmware release notes for fixes specifically related to stability, restart problems or hardware compatibility.
An older BIOS version is not automatically the cause of unexpected restarts.
Do not attempt a firmware update if the computer cannot maintain reliable power and the manufacturer's procedure does not provide a safe recovery method.
If there is a relevant update and a safe way to apply it, proceed according to the manufacturer instructions.

updateFirmware.title: Apply relevant firmware update
body: Confirm that the firmware update is intended for the exact computer or motherboard model.
Review the manufacturer's release notes and update instructions.
Ensure the computer has reliable power before starting the update.
For laptops, meet the manufacturer's charger and battery requirements.
If BitLocker is enabled, confirm the recovery key is available and follow manufacturer guidance about suspending protection.
Do not interrupt the firmware update.
Restart and test stability after updating.
If the computer may unexpectedly lose power, do not perform the update without an appropriate safe recovery procedure.

hardwareEscalation.title: Further hardware diagnostics required
body: Unexpected restarts continue after checking available event logs, temperatures, power, memory, drivers, storage and relevant firmware.
Possible causes include motherboard faults, CPU or GPU instability, intermittent power delivery and other hardware failures.
Review any WHEA hardware errors, stop codes or memory dump files that were recorded.
For desktop computers, isolate components with known-working compatible replacements where practical.
Check motherboard diagnostic indicators and manufacturer hardware tests.
Avoid replacing expensive components based only on symptoms or an Event ID 41 entry.
Record the restart pattern, relevant logs, component specifications and troubleshooting results before arranging advanced diagnostics.
